On-Policy Transition Distillation

Runyang You  Yongqi Li\advisor Tiezheng Yu  Wenjie Li Affiliation: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University   Huawei Technologies Ltd.
runyang.y@outlook.com, liyongqi0@gmail.com
Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates expert capabilities into a single student by matching teacher and student final-layer distributions on student-generated rollouts. We investigate whether depthwise prediction transitions, the changes in predictions between layers, can provide additional task-relevant supervision. Our diagnostic study finds that stronger teacher–student agreement in intermediate transitions is associated with higher answer correctness within questions, with correct responses exhibiting lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. These observations motivate On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which augments final-layer distribution matching by aligning teacher and student layer-to-layer log-probability increments on student-generated rollouts. Evaluations across three backbones and eight benchmarks spanning mathematics, coding, and instruction following show that OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation. In the three-domain setting, OPTD recovers ≈90%\approx 90\% of the overall teacher–student capability gap, compared with ≈75%\approx 75\% for OPD.

1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a core post-training recipe for consolidating specialized capabilities from expert teachers into a unified student, as exemplified by DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5 [1, 2]. Specifically, it applies dense supervision at every token position of a student-generated rollout by comparing the teacher’s and student’s distributions conditioned on the same prefix, and uses the resulting KL-derived token-level reward to guide policy distillation [3]. Grounding supervision in the student’s own rollouts, OPD alleviates exposure bias [4], mitigates catastrophic forgetting [2], and learns with substantially fewer samples than outcome-reward RL [5].

OPD methods typically transfer knowledge by solely aligning the student’s final-layer prediction distribution with those of the teacher. The final-layer distribution, however, represents only the endpoint of the teacher’s decision process. Recent studies show that these predictions develop through successive prediction revisions across depth: early layers can favor statistical guesses that deeper layers refine as contextual information develops [6, 7]. Layer-contrastive decoding further demonstrates that differences between predictions across depths, which we term depthwise prediction transitions, can be exploited to improve generation factuality [8]. This raises a natural question: can such transitions provide additional task-relevant guidance for on-policy distillation?

To answer this question, we start by comparing teacher–student agreement on correct and incorrect student-generated responses, and found that stronger teacher–student agreement in intermediate prediction transitions is associated with higher answer correctness, while final-layer agreement exhibits the opposite trend (Fig. 1(a)). This correctness-related pattern extends across all measured intermediate layer pairs: correct responses exhibit lower mean transition KL, with larger relative gaps for transitions involving middle-to-late layers (Fig. 1(b)). Together, these findings motivate distilling the teacher’s internal predictive changes alongside its final output distribution.

We therefore propose On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which complements final-layer supervision with alignment of teacher–student predictive transitions on student-generated rollouts, as illustrated in Fig. On-Policy Transition Distillation(b). Rather than aligning only the final-layer distributions as in Fig. On-Policy Transition Distillation(a), OPTD examines the prediction changes between selected anchor layers for the same student-visited prefix. For each candidate token, these changes are represented by the layer-to-layer increment in its log probability, capturing both the direction and magnitude of the prediction revision across depth. We then compare the teacher’s and student’s increments and use their discrepancy as a reward alongside the final-layer OPD objective, encouraging agreement with the teacher’s predictive changes on the same student-generated trajectory.

Evaluations across three model backbones, three domains, and eight benchmarks show that OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation. Under matched training budgets, it consistently improves overall performance over standard OPD across all evaluated backbones and domain settings, supporting the joint transfer of heterogeneous specialist capabilities into a single student. In the three-domain setting, OPTD recovers ≈90%\approx 90\% of the overall teacher–student capability gap, compared with ≈75%\approx 75\% for OPD (Tab. 2). Internal diagnostics further show that transition supervision improves alignment with the teacher across depth, including intermediate-layer predictions and the final output.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We characterize the relationship between teacher–student agreement and answer correctness across model depth, identifying a correctness-related pattern in intermediate predictive transitions that motivates transition-based supervision.

  • •

    We propose On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which transfers the teacher’s depthwise prediction refinement by aligning the direction and magnitude of cross-layer prediction increments on student-generated rollouts.

  • •

    We demonstrate that OPTD achieves optimal overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation, consistently improving over OPD across backbones and domain settings.

2 Preliminaries and Motivating Observations

We first review on-policy distillation (OPD) in §2.1. We then revisit the assumption underlying standard OPD supervision and compare final-layer output agreement with depthwise transition agreement in §2.2.1. Empirical findings are summarized in §2.2.2.

2.1 On-Policy Distillation

OPD trains a student πθS\pi^{S}_{\theta} using teacher feedback on its own trajectories. 2.2 Revisiting Teacher Agreement in On-Policy Distillation

Predictions are progressively refined across transformer layers [6, 7]. We investigate whether teacher–student agreement in these predictive changes is associated with answer correctness, and how the relationship varies across depth. We use final-layer agreement as a reference.

2.2.1 Diagnostic Setup

Final-Layer Output Divergence.

We quantify final-layer teacher agreement using the trajectory-averaged reverse KL divergence:

𝒟final(y)=1T∑t=1TDKL(πθS(⋅∣st)∥πT(⋅∣st)).\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{final}}(y)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi^{S}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\,\middle\|\,\pi^{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\right). (5)
Depthwise Transition Divergence.

A model’s final prediction represents the culmination of layered computation. Across network layers, token predictions undergo progressive revisions, forming depthwise prediction transitions. Let pℓ,tSp^{S}_{\ell,t} and pℓ,tTp^{T}_{\ell,t} denote the intermediate next-token probability distributions obtained by applying the unembedding head to the layer-ℓ\ell hidden states (i.e., the logit lens) for the student and teacher, respectively, where ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\} and LL denotes the final layer. For two layers ℓ<ℓ′\ell<\ell^{\prime}, we characterize the revision in candidate log-probabilities by the prediction increment:

Δℓ→ℓ′,tS/T​(v)=log⁡pℓ′,tS/T​(v)−log⁡pℓ,tS/T​(v).\Delta^{S/T}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}(v)=\log p^{S/T}_{\ell^{\prime},t}(v)-\log p^{S/T}_{\ell,t}(v). (6)

To evaluate whether the student follows the teacher’s internal revision trajectory over the vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}, we normalize the increments into a probability distribution:

qℓ→ℓ′,tS/T​(v)=exp⁡(Δℓ→ℓ′,tS/T​(v))∑j∈𝒱exp⁡(Δℓ→ℓ′,tS/T​(j)).q^{S/T}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}(v)=\frac{\exp(\Delta^{S/T}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}(v))}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(\Delta^{S/T}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}(j))}. (7)

This distribution assigns higher probability mass to candidate tokens whose probabilities increase by a larger factor between the layers. We then measure transition divergence between layers ℓ\ell and ℓ′\ell^{\prime} using response-averaged reverse KL:

𝒟trans​(ℓ,ℓ′,y)=1T​∑t=1TDKL​(qℓ→ℓ′,tS∥qℓ→ℓ′,tT).\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{trans}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime};y)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q^{S}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}\,\middle\|\,q^{T}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}\right). (8)

A lower value of 𝒟trans​(ℓ,ℓ′,y)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{trans}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime};y) indicates that the student’s internal prediction transitions follow the teacher’s revision trajectory more faithfully.

Comparison Protocol.

We analyze 480 responses from 60 mathematics questions that elicit both correct and incorrect answers from an OPD-trained Qwen3-4B student. To compare responses to the same question, we rank its answers by transition agreement, defined as the negative mean divergence over the measured intermediate layer pairs, and report correctness across four agreement groups (Fig. 1(a)). We repeat this ranking using negative final-layer KL as a reference. To examine the depthwise pattern, we compare correct and incorrect responses at each layer pair (Fig. 1(b)). Let 𝒟¯correct\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathrm{correct}} and 𝒟¯incorrect\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathrm{incorrect}} denote the respective group means, aggregated within questions and then across benchmarks. We report their relative gap:

Δ​𝒟=𝒟¯incorrect−𝒟¯correct𝒟¯correct×100%.\Delta\mathcal{D}=\frac{\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathrm{incorrect}}-\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathrm{correct}}}{\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathrm{correct}}}\times 100\%. (9)

Positive values indicate closer teacher agreement on correct responses. The checkpoint, layer pairs, aggregation, and uncertainty estimation are detailed in App. C.6.

2.2.2 Observation and Analysis

Observation 1: Agreement in predictive transitions tracks answer correctness.

Agreement with the teacher’s intermediate predictive changes carries a task-relevant signal: among responses to the same question, those with stronger transition agreement tend to be more accurate (Fig. 1(a)). Correctness rises from 38.4% in the lowest-agreement quartile to 54.1% in the highest, with similar rates in the two middle quartiles. This association links response correctness to how closely the student follows the teacher’s predictive changes across depth, motivating transitions as a candidate distillation target. Final-layer agreement exhibits the opposite trend in the same response cohort.

Observation 2: The correctness contrast is structured across depth.

The correctness-related contrast extends across all 36 measured intermediate layer pairs: correct responses exhibit lower mean transition KL than incorrect responses (Fig. 1(b)). Within this internal grid, the relative gaps are more pronounced for transitions involving middle-to-late layers. Transitions ending at the final output exhibit the opposite direction, distinguishing the internal pattern from the changes leading to the output distribution. This depthwise structure is consistent with accounts of predictions being progressively refined as contextual information develops across transformer layers [6, 7]. It motivates examining the teacher’s internal predictive changes as a task-relevant aspect of its behavior.

Together, these findings motivate distilling the teacher’s predictive changes across depth in addition to its final output distribution. We therefore introduce OPTD, which augments final-layer distribution matching with supervision on depthwise prediction transitions.

3 On-Policy Transition Distillation

Building on the observations, we propose On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD) to distill the teacher’s depthwise prediction increments from on policy rollouts.

Consider an ordered sequence of anchor layers ℓ0<ℓ1<⋯<ℓM=L\ell_{0}<\ell_{1}<\dots<\ell_{M}=L. For each segment ii, from ℓi−1\ell_{i-1} to ℓi\ell_{i}, the prediction increment Δi,tS/T​(v)\Delta^{S/T}_{i,t}(v) is the quantity defined in Eq. (6). Following the top-KK setting introduced in Section 2, we apply the same reward-weighted update to these depthwise increments. The transition-level reward is

Ri,ttrans​(v)=Δi,tT​(v)−Δi,tS​(v).R^{\mathrm{trans}}_{i,t}(v)=\Delta^{T}_{i,t}(v)-\Delta^{S}_{i,t}(v). (10)

For the segment ending at ℓi\ell_{i}, the student probabilities of the retained candidates are renormalized at the destination layer:

wi,t​(v)=pℓi,tS​(v)∑u∈𝒦tpℓi,tS​(u),v∈𝒦t.w_{i,t}(v)=\frac{p^{S}_{\ell_{i},t}(v)}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{K}_{t}}p^{S}_{\ell_{i},t}(u)},\qquad v\in\mathcal{K}_{t}. (11)

Using the detached transition signal and weights, the transition loss is

ℒtrans=−𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθS​[𝔼t​[1M​∑i=1M∑v∈𝒦twi,t​(v)​Ri,ttrans​(v)​Δi,tS​(v)]].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}}=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi^{S}_{\theta}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{K}_{t}}w_{i,t}(v)\,R^{\mathrm{trans}}_{i,t}(v)\,\Delta^{S}_{i,t}(v)\right]\right].

 (12)

During training, we retain the inherited final-layer update and add the transition update above ∇θJ=∇θJOPD+∇θJtrans\nabla_{\theta}J=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{OPD}}+\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{trans}}. The relation between this practical update and the exact reverse transition-KL gradient is derived in App. B.4; implementation details are given in App. B.

4 Experiment Setup

We evaluate OPTD in dual-domain (§5.1) and three-domain (§5.2) distillation settings, covering mathematics and coding, with instruction following added in the latter. Each prompt receives supervision from its corresponding domain specialist, following the protocol described in§2.1.

Datasets and Benchmarks.

We train on DAPO-Math-17k [11] and DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset [12]. We evaluate mathematics on AIME24/25 [13] and AIMO [14]; coding on LiveCodeBench v5 [15], CodeContests [16], and Codeforces with CodeElo [17]. For instruction following, we use Rubrics-To-Tokens [18] for training and IFEval [19] for evaluation. Training prompts are sampled equally across domains.

Models.

We use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B [20] and Qwen3-4B [5] as students, each supervised by domain specialists detailed in App. C.2.

Baselines.

We compare OPTD with OPD and its latent-supervision variants, OPRD [21] and LastOPD [22], which transfer teacher knowledge through hidden representations. We also implement LayerOPD: an absolute-layer supervision baseline that applies OPD across corresponding intermediate layer readouts.

Training.

Methods within each setting share the student initialization, teachers, data, and update budget: 150 updates for 1.5B, 50 for 4B, and 100 for 7B. We use a learning rate of 10−510^{-5} and two on-policy responses per prompt. Qwen3-4B uses non-thinking mode, while the R1-Distill students use reasoning prompts.

Evaluation.

We report Avg@16 for mathematics, Avg@8/Pass@8 for LiveCodeBench, Avg@16 for CodeContests, estimated Codeforces Elo, and average strict/loose IFEval accuracy under 16 samples per question. Dataset links, baseline implementations, and detailed training and evaluation settings are provided in App. C.

5 Main Results

5.1 Results on Dual-Domain Setting

Table 1 evaluates whether depthwise transition supervision improves the joint transfer of mathematics and coding capabilities under matched training settings.

  • •

    Transition supervision improves overall capability transfer across model sizes. The best OPTD configuration achieves the highest Overall score at each of the three model sizes, tying LayerOPD at 4B. At 4B, for example, Late OPTD raises Overall from 33.77% to 34.68% and improves all three mathematics benchmark averages over OPD. At 7B, it improves both Math Avg and Coding Avg over OPD, raising Overall from 49.14% to 50.06%. These results support transition supervision as a useful addition to final-output distillation for consolidating specialist capabilities in a single student. The preferred supervision depth depends on the setting: Middle OPTD leads at 1.5B, whereas Late OPTD leads at 4B and 7B.

  • •

    Representation alignment is effective, but its gains can involve cross-domain tradeoffs. Representation-based supervision can enhance capability transfer: LastOPD improves Overall over OPD at all three sizes and achieves the highest Coding Avg at 1.5B and 4B, while OPRD improves both domain averages over OPD at 4B. However, LastOPD’s coding gains at 1.5B and 4B accompany lower Math Avg than OPD in both settings. This pattern illustrates a cross-domain tradeoff: stronger transfer in one domain does not necessarily translate into stronger transfer in the other. For multi-specialist distillation, these results motivate assessing representation alignment through joint capability transfer, since a leading domain-specific score can coexist with a tradeoff elsewhere.

5.2 Results on Three-Domain Setting

We extend distillation to a 1.5B student with specialist teachers for mathematics, coding, and instruction following. Table 2 compares OPD and OPTD under identical update budgets.

  • •

    The benefits of transition supervision extend to heterogeneous capabilities. OPTD improves every reported mathematics and instruction-following metric over OPD, with instruction-following gains spanning both IFEval and IFBench. These simultaneous improvements raise Overall from 37.89% to 39.57%. The results extend the evidence for OPTD beyond math/coding distillation: transition supervision also supports the integration of instruction-following capabilities alongside specialist reasoning skills in one student.

  • •

    OPTD recovers more of the specialist capabilities left untapped by OPD. OPD already reaches the coding teacher’s domain average, while recovering 70.1% and 65.0% of the teacher–student gaps in mathematics and instruction following, respectively. OPTD increases these recovery rates to 85.7% and 74.8%, while retaining a coding domain average above the teacher reference. Thus, the overall improvement reflects additional transfer in the domains with larger remaining teacher gaps, alongside sustained specialist-level coding performance.

These results support capability transfer from heterogeneous specialists; complete results appear in App. A.2 and Tabs. 8–10.

6 Further Analysis

This section examines the design and mechanism of transition supervision. We study how transition geometry affect transfer, how alternative objective formulations compare, and whether OPTD improves the student’s internal prediction alignment with the teacher. Further diagnostic and derivational analyses are provided in Apps. D and B.4.

6.1 Transition Geometry Analysis

We examine how the placement and span of a supervised transition path affect capability transfer in the 1.5B multi-domain setting, where Math is the average of AIME24, AIME25, and AIMO; Coding is LiveCodeBench, and IF is accuracy on IFEval. We express depth as r=ℓ/Lr=\ell/L, where L=28L=28 for this backbone, with the final prediction at r=1r=1. We define placement as the normalized depth cc of the central supervised block and span as the normalized distance ss from that block to each neighboring block. Given center cc and span ss, the intermediate readouts are positioned at (c−s,c,c+s)(c-s,c,c+s). Early, Middle, and Late placements have centers at approximately 0.3930.393, 0.4640.464, and 0.5360.536, respectively. Under otherwise matched training conditions (§4), we first compare placements at a fixed span of s≈0.214s\approx 0.214, then compare spans of approximately 0.1430.143, 0.2140.214, and 0.2860.286 at the Middle and Late placements. Exact block indices are provided in App. C.3.

  • •

    The best placement depends on the target domain. At a fixed span of s≈0.214s\approx 0.214 (Tab. 3), Middle achieves the highest Math score, whereas Late achieves the highest Coding and IF scores and the highest overall score. Thus, placement affects which capabilities benefit most from transition supervision, with Late providing the strongest joint transfer in this comparison.

  • •

    Compact paths achieve the best overall performance. The compact span s≈0.143s\approx 0.143 achieves the highest average at both Middle and Late (Tab. 4). Relative to s≈0.286s\approx 0.286, it raises the average by 0.97 at Middle and 1.51 at Late, improving all three domain scores at both placements. This repeated pattern supports supervising more local prediction revisions rather than spanning a broader depth interval in these settings.

The compact Late path achieves the highest overall score in this sweep (46.76%), supporting its use in the main three-domain experiment. Its intermediate readouts lie at approximately (0.393,0.536,0.679)(0.393,0.536,0.679), with center c≈0.536c\approx 0.536 and span s≈0.143s\approx 0.143.

6.2 Objective Formulation Analysis

Our motivating analysis uses transition KL to measure agreement between normalized prediction increments. We now examine how to turn this transition signal into a training update, comparing direct transition-KL minimization with OPTD’s OPD-style formulation. ReverseKL uses increment-softmax weights qSq^{S} and a centered transition reward (App. B.4); OPTD uses destination-layer predictive weights wi,tw_{i,t} and the raw transition reward Ri,ttransR^{\mathrm{trans}}_{i,t} (Eqs. (10)–(12)). Two hybrid variants pair increment weights with the raw reward and predictive weights with the qSq^{S}-centered reward, respectively. We compare all four formulations under controlled conditions in the 1.5B dual-domain setting.

  • •

    OPTD improves both domains over direct transition-KL matching. OPTD achieves the highest average in Table 5 (36.35%), improving on ReverseKL by 0.23 percentage points in Math and 0.53 points in Coding. Its overall gain therefore reflects improvements in both domains, supporting the OPD-style transition update for capability transfer in this setting.

  • •

    Raw rewards work better with predictive weights. To test OPTD’s choice of raw transition rewards, we hold predictive weights fixed and introduce reward centering. The raw-reward update achieves an average of 36.35%, whereas the centered variant reaches 21.75%. Under increment weights, however, centered and raw rewards yield similar averages, locating the adverse effect of centering in its pairing with predictive weights in this comparison. The gradient analysis in App. D.2 further shows very large gradient norms for the centered predictive variant, indicating optimization instability during training. These results support retaining raw transition rewards when using OPTD’s predictive weights.

These comparisons support OPTD’s pairing of destination-layer predictive weights with the raw transition reward.

6.3 Internal Alignment Analysis

We examine whether OPTD produces the intended transition alignment and whether this improvement also appears in layer predictions. We compare OPD, LayerOPD, and OPTD under controlled conditions on Qwen3-4B, evaluating all three on the same saved rollout texts.

We measure student-to-teacher KL for layer predictions (curves) and teacher-to-student KL for normalized prediction increments (bars). The shared-text protocol and score averaging are detailed in App. C.7. Fig. 2 reports percentage reductions over OPD; larger values indicate closer agreement with the teacher.

  • •

    OPTD achieves closer transition alignment than LayerOPD. Across all plotted intermediate-layer intervals, OPTD reduces transition KL by roughly 26%–44% over OPD, compared with about 5%–14% for LayerOPD. The consistently larger reductions show that transition supervision brings the student’s depthwise prediction revisions closer to the teacher’s than direct alignment of layer predictions does.

  • •

    Transition supervision also improves prediction alignment across depth. OPTD reduces layer-wise prediction reverse KL by roughly 32%–42% at intermediate readouts and by 12.7% at the final output. These reductions exceed LayerOPD’s at every plotted readout, including its 2.2% final-output reduction. Thus, supervising how predictions change across layers also improves agreement with the teacher’s prediction states, extending the observed alignment benefit beyond the transitions themselves.

Together, these observations support teacher-guided prediction revisions as an effective target for transferring knowledge across depth.

7 Related Work

On-Policy Distillation.

Knowledge distillation transfers teacher capabilities through predictive distributions or sequences [23, 24]. To alleviate exposure bias from offline demonstrations [25], on-policy distillation (OPD) queries the teacher on student rollouts for dense step-level supervision [26, 3, 27, 4, 9]. While standard OPD optimizes final-layer distributions, complementary approaches align heterogeneous intermediate hidden states through projection heads or staged schedules [28, 29, 21, 22]. However, cross-architecture matching requires careful projection designs, while static feature alignment captures proximity rather than the formation and revision of predictive beliefs across layers.

Depthwise Computation and Prediction Dynamics.

A language model’s final output represents the endpoint of hierarchical computations, while vocabulary lenses reveal a depthwise trajectory of hypothesis formation and refinement [6, 30]. Transformer layers introduce geometric displacements that eliminate surface-level lexical fallacies and resolve reasoning dependencies across depth [31, 32, 7]. Recent analyses show that layer-to-layer transitions convey correctness signals separating valid reasoning from spurious correlations [31]. However, depthwise transitions remain predominantly studied through post-hoc interpretability; their potential as on-policy supervision signals for transferring teacher reasoning dynamics remains underexplored.

8 Conclusion and Future Work

We studied depthwise prediction transitions as a source of supervision for on-policy distillation. Our diagnostic analysis links stronger teacher–student agreement in intermediate transitions to higher answer correctness, with correct responses exhibiting lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. Motivated by these observations, we proposed On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which complements final-layer distribution matching by aligning teacher–student prediction changes across depth on student-generated rollouts. Across three backbones, three domains, and eight benchmarks, OPTD achieves the optimal overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation, which demonstrates the value of depthwise transition supervision for consolidating specialist capabilities. Future work could explore how depthwise transitions can provide supervision for general reinforcement learning.

Appendix A Detailed Evaluation Results

A.1 Student and Teacher Reference Performance

Tab. 6 reports the initial students and their domain teachers before distillation. Model identities are given in Tab. 11. The mathematics scores provide the reference anchors for teacher-gap recovery. Each specialist is reported on its corresponding domain.

A.2 Full Multi-Domain Results

Tabs. 8–10 present the complete evaluation suite across mathematics, coding, and instruction following in the multi-domain setting. They include detailed breakdowns for AIMO, CodeContests, CodeElo, and individual prompt/instruction criteria on IFEval and IFBench.

Appendix B Method Implementation and Derivation

We compare the candidate-based final-policy OPD update with the transition update used by OPTD. Both use student-generated prefixes and fixed teacher predictions. In the pseudocode below, detach() preserves a tensor’s value while preventing gradients through that occurrence. All softmax operations and candidate sums act on the last dimension. Log-probabilities are computed over the full vocabulary before candidates are selected.

B.1 Final-Policy OPD

The following pseudocode shows the student-top-kk formulation. The teacher is evaluated on the same candidate tokens as the student. For readability, logits below include any configured temperature scaling.

student_log_probs = log_softmax(student_logits)
teacher_log_probs = log_softmax(teacher_logits)

candidate_ids = student_logits.topk(top_k).indices
student_candidate_log_probs = gather(
    student_log_probs, candidate_ids
)
teacher_candidate_log_probs = gather(
    teacher_log_probs, candidate_ids
)

weights = softmax(
    student_candidate_log_probs.detach()
)
score_coeff = (
    weights
    * (student_candidate_log_probs.detach()
       - teacher_candidate_log_probs.detach())
).detach()

per_token_loss = (
    score_coeff * student_candidate_log_probs
).sum(dim=-1)

B.2 OPTD

For each response position, we gather the intermediate and final prediction distributions for the same candidate tokens. The tensors student_path and teacher_path have shape [batch, layer, token, candidate], with layers ordered from shallow to deep and ending at the final prediction. Candidate identities are held fixed across layers so that each subtraction compares the same token. The training update is:

teacher_delta = (
    teacher_path[:, 1:] - teacher_path[:, :-1]
).detach()
student_delta = (
    student_path[:, 1:] - student_path[:, :-1]
)

weights = softmax(student_path[:, 1:].detach())
score_coeff = (
    weights
    * (student_delta.detach() - teacher_delta)
).detach()

per_transition_token_loss = (
    score_coeff * student_delta
).sum(dim=-1)

Gradients pass through both student readouts that define each transition; the teacher increments, candidate weights, and correction coefficients are detached.

B.3 Loss Reduction

Using the candidate set 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t} from the main text, let mtm_{t} denote the response-position mask. The loss for transition ii is

ℒtrans(i)=1∑tmt​∑tmt​∑k∈𝒦twi,t​(k)​sg⁡[Δi,tS​(k)−Δi,tT​(k)]​Δi,tS​(k),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{\sum_{t}m_{t}}\sum_{t}m_{t}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{t}}w_{i,t}(k)\,\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\Delta^{S}_{i,t}(k)-\Delta^{T}_{i,t}(k)\right]\Delta^{S}_{i,t}(k),

where wi,tw_{i,t} is the destination-layer candidate weight in Eq. (11) and is held fixed during differentiation. In practice, evaluating the expectation in Eq. (12) over candidate subset 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t} restricts computation to high-probability tokens. Token losses are reduced over the retained response positions, and the selected transitions receive equal weights:

ℒtrans=1M​∑i=1Mℒtrans(i).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trans}}^{(i)}.

The transition update is combined with final-policy OPD; the executed scaling is specified in App. C.3. Each transition has its own weights and correction, so the objective preserves the contribution from every supervised layer pair.

B.4 Relation to Reverse Transition KL

The transition reward in Eq. (10) is the increment-level counterpart of the OPD reward. We derive the exact gradient of the reverse transition KL and then relate it to the detached top-KK update used in the main text.

Fix a response position tt and transition ii. Use qSq^{S} and qTq^{T} from Eq. (7), and write zkS=Δi,tS​(k)z^{S}_{k}=\Delta^{S}_{i,t}(k) and zkT=Δi,tT​(k)z^{T}_{k}=\Delta^{T}_{i,t}(k) for brevity. The reverse transition KL is

𝒦i,t=DKL(qS∥qT).\mathcal{K}_{i,t}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{S}\|q^{T}).

Because qTq^{T} is fixed, differentiating with respect to the student increments gives

∇θ𝒦i,t=∑kqkS​[(zkS−zkT)−∑jqjS​(zjS−zjT)]​∇θzkS.\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{K}_{i,t}=\sum_{k}q^{S}_{k}\left[(z^{S}_{k}-z^{T}_{k})-\sum_{j}q^{S}_{j}(z^{S}_{j}-z^{T}_{j})\right]\nabla_{\theta}z^{S}_{k}.

Defining the teacher-guided correction Rk=zkT−zkSR_{k}=z^{T}_{k}-z^{S}_{k} and its qSq^{S}-weighted mean R¯=∑jqjS​Rj\bar{R}=\sum_{j}q^{S}_{j}R_{j}, this becomes

−∇θ𝒦i,t=∑kqkS​(Rk−R¯)​∇θzkS.-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{K}_{i,t}=\sum_{k}q^{S}_{k}(R_{k}-\bar{R})\nabla_{\theta}z^{S}_{k}. (13)

Thus, a centered reward weighted by the normalized student increments gives the score-function form of reverse transition KL.

The practical OPTD update in Eq. (12) uses wi,tw_{i,t} from Eq. (11), normalized over 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t}, and the raw transition reward Ri,ttransR^{\mathrm{trans}}_{i,t} from Eq. (10). The exact reverse transition-KL gradient instead uses increment-softmax weights qSq^{S} and their centered correction. This distinction motivates the controlled formulation comparison in §6.2.

Appendix C Experimental Setup and Reproducibility

C.1 Datasets

We use DAPO-Math-17k for mathematics, DeepCoder-Preview-Dataset for coding, and Rubrics-To-Tokens for instruction following. Training prompts are sampled to give each domain equal representation. Each student-generated response is assigned to its source-domain specialist. The instruction-following teacher is added in the three-domain setting.

C.2 Students and Domain Teachers

Tab. 11 lists the student and domain teachers for each model size. The instruction-following teacher is added only in the multi-domain 1.5B setting. The link icons open the corresponding Hugging Face repositories.

C.3 Training Configuration

On-Policy Training.

The 1.5B settings use 16 rollout prompts per update and eight prompts per optimization minibatch; the 4B and 7B settings use 128 and 64, respectively. Each prompt contributes two student-generated responses, and each rollout batch supplies two optimization minibatches. Training runs for 150 updates at 1.5B, 50 at 4B, and 100 at 7B. All settings use BF16 and a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, held constant after warmup over the first 3% of training. Prompts are capped at 2,048 tokens; responses are capped at 16,384 tokens for dual-domain training and 10,240 for three-domain training.

Supervised Depth Paths.

Each OPTD path consists of three intermediate readouts followed by the final output, yielding three supervised transitions. The dual-domain comparisons use intermediate blocks 7/13/197/13/19 and 11/15/1911/15/19 at 1.5B, 7/13/197/13/19 and 14/19/2414/19/24 at 4B, and 13/17/2113/17/21 at 7B. For the 1.5B student, the main-result labels Middle and Late denote blocks 7/13/197/13/19 and 11/15/1911/15/19, respectively. The main three-domain configuration uses the latter, a compact Late path with a four-block span. In the 1.5B geometry analysis, Middle and Late denote centers at blocks 13 and 15, respectively. For a block center cbc_{b} and block span sbs_{b}, the selected blocks are (cb−sb,cb,cb+sb)(c_{b}-s_{b},c_{b},c_{b}+s_{b}); the normalized center and span are c=cb/28c=c_{b}/28 and s=sb/28s=s_{b}/28. The tested block spans are 4, 6, and 8, corresponding to normalized spans of approximately 0.1430.143, 0.2140.214, and 0.2860.286. Other paths are specified in the corresponding analyses. All block indices are zero-based. Intermediate next-token distributions are obtained by applying the model’s final normalization and shared output projection to the selected hidden states, with temperature 1.

Transition Supervision.

Final-policy OPD selects the student’s top-16 candidate tokens at each response prefix and evaluates the assigned teacher on the same candidates. OPTD retains these candidate identities across the supervised path and applies transition supervision to the last 2,000 response prediction positions, or the entire response when it is shorter. The three transition losses receive equal weight and are summed with the final-policy OPD loss, corresponding to a weight of 3 on the mean transition objective in Eq. (12). The combined loss updates the student’s intermediate representations and shared output projection, with teacher predictions and reward weights held fixed.

C.4 Baseline Implementations

All baselines share OPTD’s domain-specific teacher assignment and response supervision span (App. C.3). Where included, final-policy OPD follows the update in App. B.

OPRD.

OPRD [21] aligns ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized student and teacher hidden representations using MSE with coefficient 1. The 1.5B baseline supervises all transformer layers with this loss alone; the 4B baseline uses the same intermediate layers as OPTD’s Late path and combines representation alignment with final-policy OPD.

LastOPD.

LastOPD [22] applies the same representation loss to the final-layer hidden states. Over training, its weight decreases linearly from 1 toward 0, while the final-policy OPD weight increases from 0 toward 1.

LayerOPD.

LayerOPD combines final-policy OPD with independent alignment of the prediction distributions at three intermediate readouts. It uses the same readout construction as OPTD and selects the student’s top-16 candidates separately at each readout for both models to score. The 1.5B and 4B baselines use OPTD’s Middle and Late paths, respectively; the 7B baseline uses blocks 11/15/1911/15/19.

C.5 Benchmark Evaluation

Sampled responses use BF16 and top-p=0.95p=0.95. In the result tables, Avg denotes mean per-problem accuracy and Pass denotes the fraction of problems with at least one correct response; the number of sampled responses used to estimate each metric is specified below.

Mathematics.

AIME24 and AIME25 contain 30 problems each, and the AIMO evaluation subset contains 83 problems. We sample 16 responses per problem at temperature 0.7 with a 31,744-token output cap and score final answers using a rule-based grader. Math Avg. gives equal weight to the three benchmark Avg scores. The reference scores use non-thinking prompts for Qwen3-4B and reasoning prompts for the R1-Distill students.

Coding.

LiveCodeBench v5 uses the 279-problem DeepCoder test set at temperature 0.6. The main comparisons report Avg and Pass from eight responses per problem; the output cap is 32,768 tokens. The 1.5B reference scores combine the preserved four-response batch with an independent four-response batch under the archived four-seed protocol; the 7B reference scores use native reasoning templates. CodeContests uses 165 test problems with 16 Python 3 solutions per problem, temperature 0.7, and a 15,360-token output cap. Solutions must pass all public, private, and generated tests, with a 10-second per-test timeout and a 1,024 MiB memory limit. We report a CodeElo estimate [17] on the DeepCoder evaluation split [12], comprising 408 Codeforces problems across 57 contests, with eight responses per problem, temperature 0.6, and a 32,768-token output cap. Candidates are graded locally with SandboxFusion. Following the CodeElo methodology (Sections 3.3 and 4.1), we compute contest scores from the first accepted candidate and preceding failed attempts, estimate a rating using human contest standings and pre-contest ratings, and average the ratings across contests.11 1 https://github.com/QwenLM/CodeElo. The result is an estimate because verdicts come from local tests; the original CodeElo protocol submits solutions to the official Codeforces judge.

Instruction Following.

IFEval uses all 541 prompts with 16 responses per prompt, temperature 0.7, and a 31,744-token output cap. IFBench uses all 300 test prompts with one greedy response per prompt and the same output cap. Both benchmarks report strict and loose prompt- and instruction-level accuracies, as defined in Table 7; both models use the shared rLLM reasoning template within each benchmark.

Teacher-Gap Recovery.

Following the gap recovery rate in prior OPD work [4], we measure the fraction of the initial student–teacher performance gap closed by training:

Recovery=100×strained−sinitialsteacher−sinitial%.\mathrm{Recovery}=100\times\frac{s_{\mathrm{trained}}-s_{\mathrm{initial}}}{s_{\mathrm{teacher}}-s_{\mathrm{initial}}}\,\%.

Here, sinitials_{\mathrm{initial}}, straineds_{\mathrm{trained}}, and steachers_{\mathrm{teacher}} denote the scores of the initial student, trained student, and corresponding domain teacher under the same evaluation protocol. A recovery of 0%0\% denotes no change from the initial student; 100%100\% denotes matching the teacher, and values above 100%100\% denote surpassing it. We apply this definition to each reported metric using the reference scores in Tables 6 and 7. For aggregate scores such as Math Avg., we compute recovery from the aggregate scores themselves rather than averaging per-benchmark recovery rates.

C.6 Teacher Agreement Diagnostic

Data and Readouts.

Fig. 1 uses Qwen3-4B after 50 OPD updates and its mathematics specialist teacher in Tab. 11. We retain 60 questions with both correct and incorrect answers among eight archived responses per question: 14 AIME24, 13 AIME25, and 33 AIMO questions, totaling 480 responses. Divergences follow Eqs. (5) and (8), using full-vocabulary student-to-teacher KL averaged over response positions. Intermediate predictions use each model’s final normalization and unembedding head; final readouts use the already normalized hidden state. Figure layer labels are zero-based decoder block indices.

Agreement and Correctness (Panel a).

Transition agreement is the negative arithmetic mean of transition KL over all 36 layer pairs among blocks 5,7,…,215,7,\ldots,21; final-layer agreement is negative final-output KL. We rank each question’s eight responses separately by each metric and divide them into four groups of two, from lowest to highest agreement. For each group, we average correctness within questions, then across questions within each benchmark, and finally equally across the three benchmarks. Shading denotes pointwise 95% percentile intervals from 10,000 question-bootstrap resamples stratified by benchmark (seed 20261013), retaining all responses and group assignments of each sampled question. Lines connect the observed group means.

Correctness Contrast across Depth (Panel b).

We evaluate all 45 layer pairs among blocks 5,7,…,215,7,\ldots,21 and the final readout. For each pair, divergences are averaged separately over correct and incorrect responses within each question, then across questions within each benchmark, and finally equally across benchmarks. The heatmap reports the relative gap in Eq. (9), computed from these aggregated group means.

C.7 Internal Alignment Evaluation

The analysis in §6.3 compares Qwen3-4B OPD, LayerOPD, and OPTD at 50 updates under shared token contexts. We select 12 questions from each of AIME24, AIME25, and AIMO without filtering by correctness or response length. Each question contributes one OPD response and one OPTD response, giving 36 questions and 72 texts. All three students and the teacher process the same prompt–response sequences, so alignment is measured at identical contexts.

We measure both layer predictions and prediction transitions over the full vocabulary at all response token positions. Intermediate predictions are obtained using each model’s own final normalization and LM head. The layer-prediction curves in Fig. 2 report student-to-teacher KL, DKL(pℓ,tS∥pℓ,tT)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{S}_{\ell,t}\|p^{T}_{\ell,t}), at zero-based blocks 0,4,8,12,16,20,24,28,320,4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32 and the final output. The transition bars report teacher-to-student KL, DKL(qℓ→ℓ′,tT∥qℓ→ℓ′,tS)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{T}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}\|q^{S}_{\ell\rightarrow\ell^{\prime},t}), using the normalized increments in Eq. (7) between adjacent intermediate readouts from block 4 to block 32. Readouts are positioned at normalized depth r=ℓ/36r=\ell/36, with the final output placed at r=1r=1.

For each readout or interval, we first average KL over response positions within each text, then over the two response sources within each question. We average questions within each benchmark and give the three benchmarks equal weight. The plotted reduction is 100​(1−method distance/OPD distance)100(1-\text{method distance}/\text{OPD distance}), computed from these aggregate distances; positive values indicate closer teacher alignment than OPD.

The layer-prediction curves include 95% percentile intervals from 20,000 paired question-bootstrap resamples. Questions are resampled within each benchmark, keeping both response sources and all students paired, and the aggregate reduction is recomputed in each resample.

Appendix D Additional Analyses

D.1 Final-Output Agreement Across Training

We examine whether the final-output pattern in §2.2.2 is already present early in training. This supplementary analysis follows a Qwen3-4B OPD run trained on a fixed pool of 1,200 mathematics and 1,200 coding prompts, evaluating after 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 updates. At each stage, we use the first eight archived responses per mathematics question and all four responses per LiveCodeBench question, retaining questions with both correct and incorrect answers. We compute full-vocabulary student-to-teacher reverse KL on student-generated prefixes, average over response tokens and then responses within each correctness group, and weight questions equally within each benchmark.

Fig. 3 shows lower mean KL for incorrect responses on all four benchmarks at every evaluated stage. The pattern is already pronounced on AIME24 after 10 updates (50.6% lower), while AIME25 is nearly tied at this stage (0.8% lower). By 50 updates, incorrect responses have lower KL by 46.5%, 18.8%, 29.0%, and 38.9% on AIME24, AIME25, AIMO, and LiveCodeBench, respectively. The size of the difference varies across benchmarks and need not increase monotonically with training.

To check whether these changes arise solely from changes in the question set, we also restrict each benchmark to questions with mixed outcomes at all five stages: 9 AIME24, 7 AIME25, 17 AIMO, and 12 LiveCodeBench questions. On these fixed question sets, the lower-KL pattern remains present in every benchmark at every stage. From 10 to 50 updates, the relative reduction grows from 4.4% to 26.2% on AIME25, from 12.4% to 24.6% on AIMO, and from 14.9% to 39.4% on LiveCodeBench; AIME24 remains pronounced at 50.7% and 48.1%, respectively. These observations show that the motivating phenomenon extends across training stages, while its evolution is benchmark-dependent.

D.2 Predictive Weights and Reward Centering

The Predictive weights + centered reward ablation in §6.2 combines destination-layer predictive weights with the transition reward centered under qSq^{S}. We examine how this pairing changes the update coefficients. For one transition and one response position, let Rk=zkT−zkSR_{k}=z^{T}_{k}-z^{S}_{k} and define

R¯q=∑kqkS​Rk.\bar{R}_{q}=\sum_{k}q^{S}_{k}R_{k}.

The centered predictive-weighted coefficient is

Ckpred+center=−wi,t​(k)​(Rk−R¯q),C^{\mathrm{pred+center}}_{k}=-w_{i,t}(k)(R_{k}-\bar{R}_{q}),

whereas OPTD’s raw predictive-weighted coefficient is

Ckpred=−wi,t​(k)​Rk.C^{\mathrm{pred}}_{k}=-w_{i,t}(k)R_{k}.

Their difference is an additional term proportional to the predictive weights:

Ckpred+center−Ckpred=wi,t​(k)​R¯q.C^{\mathrm{pred+center}}_{k}-C^{\mathrm{pred}}_{k}=w_{i,t}(k)\bar{R}_{q}.

The reverse-KL gradient is centered under qSq^{S} and therefore satisfies ∑kqkS​(Rk−R¯q)=0\sum_{k}q^{S}_{k}(R_{k}-\bar{R}_{q})=0. The predictive-weighted coefficient instead has

∑kwi,t​(k)​(Rk−R¯q)=∑kwi,t​(k)​Rk−∑kqkS​Rk,\displaystyle\sum_{k}w_{i,t}(k)(R_{k}-\bar{R}_{q})=\sum_{k}w_{i,t}(k)R_{k}-\sum_{k}q^{S}_{k}R_{k},

which is generally nonzero. Centering under qSq^{S} therefore adds wi,t​(k)​R¯qw_{i,t}(k)\bar{R}_{q} to the raw predictive-weighted coefficient. The resulting coefficients do not generally retain the zero-sum property of the reverse transition-KL gradient derived in App. B.4. This coefficient difference distinguishes the two updates; we next examine their gradient scales during training.

An analytical and numerical backward-pass audit confirms the implemented formulations, with maximum logit-gradient discrepancies below 10−1610^{-16}. Table 12 reports the recorded gradient scales under the matched 150-update setting.

The centered predictive branch reaches a maximum pre-clipping gradient norm of 4576, compared with 16.06 and 3.10 for the two increment-weighted branches. Together with the controlled results in Table 5, this supports pairing predictive weights with the raw transition reward in OPTD.
